Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Carbon is special because it can form four covalent bonds and link with other carbon atoms in long chains, branches and rings (a property called catenation), giving a vast number of compounds. Examples of organic compounds include methane, ethanol and glucose. Important sources are petroleum (crude oil) and natural gas, which are very significant to Nigeria's economy.

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, meaning they contain only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms. They form a homologous series with the general formula CnH(2n+2). The first members are methane (CH4), ethane (C2H6), propane (C3H8) and butane (C4H10). Alkanes are generally unreactive but undergo combustion (burning in air to give carbon dioxide and water) and substitution reactions with halogens. They are major components of natural gas and petroleum and are widely used as fuels.

What is the difference between alkanes and alkenes?

The key difference is the type of carbon-to-carbon bond. Alkanes are saturated: they have only single bonds (C-C) and the general formula CnH(2n+2), e.g. ethane C2H6. Alkenes are unsaturated: they contain at least one carbon-to-carbon double bond (C=C) and the general formula CnH(2n), e.g. ethene C2H4. Because of the double bond, alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and undergo addition reactions. A common test: alkenes decolourise bromine water, while alkanes do not. This test is frequently asked in WAEC.
